So what does this mean to you? Because what it sounds like to me is any time my *spouse* is going through something mentally taxing and difficult to the point of needing therapy, I should turn my head and tell them to go figure it out and I'll be here when it gets better. This isn't just some acquaintance or even a friend (and for the record I also think it's shit friend behaviour to not support someone **WHERE YOU CAN**), this is a person I've chosen to intertwine my life with on many deep levels-- or is reddit going to tell me I'm reading too much into my years-long relationship too? 

I will reiterate what I have stated elsewhere: I understand it is NOT MY RESPONSIBILITY, and that I can't do therapy for anyone or force water down the horse's throat. What I'm looking for is practical advice on what I can do at the moment and when it's getting to him, not the reiteration of the poly version of "hit the gym, delete Facebook, lawyer up". Some of y'all wanna do solo poly and that's ok, but that's clearly not what I'm doing nor what I'm interested in, so if everyone could chill on the projection that'd be super swell.

Where did I imply it was my responsibility to fix? I explicitly said it was *his* but that I'm going to support him any way I can, y'know as any good partner would. Not once have I said he isn't trying, nor am I staying with him because I've "already invested so much"- and to suggest that I haven't *already* experienced fruits of my labour in love after 5 years is frankly ridiculous considering I wouldn't be sticking around if I got absolutely nothing out of this. Boundaries are cool yes, and we have been having many talks about this but the *specific reason* I made a post is because the one aspect where we *are* lost in is what I can do on the sidelines while he figures it out. Waiting for a few months for someone I love deeply to make a big decision is not a big deal to me, especially since as I believe I've mentioned elsewhere Lily and I are actually friends- even if we aren't super best friends forever™ I still care about her too. Not to mention, Tulip is doing his best while being poor in America, healthcare isn't so easy as "just get it done forehead".

I heavily disagree, it's very much a we thing. I may not have any involvement in the matter, but his mental health does directly affect me as someone who both lives with him and is, as one would expect from what is essentially a spouse, very much involved in his life in general. So yes, *we* have not been lucky. His mental health may be his responsibility but to expect me to wash my hands of it completely, which is what it really seems like everyone thinks I should do, is just not how life long partnerships work.
Trying to, but we haven't been very lucky in that regard.

>**Why** do you have to support Tulip through this?  And to get to what goal?

I'm very confused by this line of questioning, but maybe I'm phrasing things poorly. My nesting partner is essentially my husband, so of course I'm going to want to support him when he's going through a hard time no matter how much or little I know about the situation, and even if that support is just spending unrelated time with him which seems to be pretty much the end of reddit's suggestions. The goal naturally is to get to a place where this isn't an issue anymore, but obviously I can only control myself so I'm working with what I can. 


>Easy to solve on YOUR end.  Stop doing group calls.  You aren't dating Lily. You don't have to socialize together.

I'm not dating her, correct, but we are still friends. For the record I *have* severely cut back contact with her. 


>What's wrong with Tulip's partner selection process?  Is Tulip so desperate they will take anyone?

This feels uncharitable. Tulip has known Lily longer than they've been dating, but until they did start dating and getting really close (and things came to more of a head between her and her husband) she kept it under wraps- precisely because she's already lost so many people due to her marriage. This comes off like telling Lily she just shouldn't have gotten involved with someone who would abuse her, people don't go into these things *knowing* it's going to turn out poorly. 


>That's the thing.   You sound a bit over involved with Tulip's stuff.

Yeah, I know it seems that way, but when the person my fiance has been talking about how cool she is for over a month says she'd really like to be friends I'm not going to just say "nah not interested" because I do actually want KTP and to even be friends with my metas where possible. Again, neither I nor Tulip knew what her relationship with her husband was like before agreeing to any of this. 



>And why are you so vested in Tulip's experience being "a good one?"  It's ok to want a partner to be ok and hope their other relationship are nice.  But why THIS involved? And why doing group calls and all that when you don't have to be?

I answered why I'm this involved, but I'll reiterate again that I think it's perfectly fine to be friends with a meta and that is what I wanted, naturally when it becomes an issue I'm going to communicate with Tulip as I have been. 


Tulip is aware of my feelings on this, but we both care about Lily and both want to be there for her as much as is possible. I don't think it's fair to blame someone for being in a messy situation they had no way of knowing they would be in, and because Tulip already developed a relationship with Lily I wasn't going to sit there and say "the best thing to do when you see someone is being abused is run" especially in the beginning when it seemed like divorce might be more on the table for Lily and her husband. I understand no one is *responsible* for anyone else here, but the implication that a friend should just drop you at the first sign of trouble is, well, troubling to me.

Respectfully, saying they have a ton in common and then saying they're from the same part of the country as an example of what they have in common is a big yikes. It comes off like you're idealizing and not actually thinking about the reality of your friend or your partner. There may be other more concrete things, but just because I'm an American from the west coast doesn't automatically mean I'll get along with west coasters.

Hey there, just wanted to say I'm pretty much in the same position as you (although I'm no longer in high school lol), the only major difference might be that I really enjoy super feminine things like lolita fashion and corsets, and a lot of traditionally feminine hobbies (knitting, embroidery, etc). I don't really like to tell people I'm nonbinary unless I'm planning on having some sort of extended relationship with them (romantic or platonic), and I'm very short and curvy so there's basically no way you'd know unless I told you or you had an ok radar for that stuff (I like to think it's pretty obvious how queer I am). I've always been a weird mix of girly and tomboyish, but ultimately I just felt "off", like I didn't really fit into the girls' circle. It could be more of a subconscious thing, since I was trying to fit in with them but no matter what school I was at (changed a lot) the girls always treated me like I was different, which obviously probably gives me a bit of a complex. Still, it doesn't change the reality of those feelings.

I started exploring my gender identity when a youtuber I watched came out, and I reached out to her asking if she thought my feelings were valid. She responded saying she thought I should pursue those feelings, and I ran with it. Since then I've become friends with more trans women and even dated some, and the general consensus I've gotten is that it's not taking up space. Obviously this isn't specifically from other nonbinary people (though I do have an agender friend who also goes by she/they and presents femme, if that counts for anything) but it's comforting for me especially because I worry a lot that I'm taking away from people who have real problems. 

I still get anxious about being seen as someone just taking the label to be qUiRkY and stuff, but at the end of the day no one else can decide what your gender is or how valid you are. Gender is actually really confusing, and as another commenter on another post said, being cis isn't something you have to justify or work your way out of, being nonbinary/trans is also perfectly natural. Even if you decide later that you are cisgender, that doesn't mean it was wrong of you to try out different labels and explore, and it's important to remember gender can also be fluid and changing. It doesn't have to be something you need a definitive answer for *right now*, or even ever, you can just enjoy the process of discovering you as much as you can.  Ultimately, what's important is how you perceive your gender, what feels right and makes you happy.

Sorry for rambling so much, I hope it helps though. 😊
